claim: More than 70% of all higher plants, including crop plants, form symbiotic associations with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF).
source: More than 70% of all higher plants, including crop plants, form symbiotic associations with arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi (AMF) (Brundrett and Tedersoo, 2018).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brundrett and Tedersoo, 2018.

claim: In AMF symbiosis, the fungus facilitates the uptake of mineral nutrients, in particular phosphorous (P) and nitrogen.
source: While the fungus facilitates the uptake of mineral nutrients, in particular phosphorous (P) and nitrogen, the plant supplies the fungus with carbon (Helber et al., 2011; Bravo et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2017; Keymer et al., 2017; Luginbuehl et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Helber et al., 2011; Bravo et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2017; Keymer et al., 2017; Luginbuehl et al., 2017).

claim: In AMF symbiosis, the plant supplies the fungus with carbon.
source: While the fungus facilitates the uptake of mineral nutrients, in particular phosphorous (P) and nitrogen, the plant supplies the fungus with carbon (Helber et al., 2011; Bravo et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2017; Keymer et al., 2017; Luginbuehl et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations (Helber et al., 2011; Bravo et al., 2017; Jiang et al., 2017; Keymer et al., 2017; Luginbuehl et al., 2017).

claim: AMF interaction affects plant growth.
source: The interaction affects plant growth (Rooney et al., 2009; Adolfsson et al., 2015) and resistance to various abiotic and biotic stresses (Pineda et al., 2010; Vannette et al., 2013; Chitarra et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Rooney et al., 2009 and Adolfsson et al., 2015.

claim: AMF interaction affects plant resistance to various abiotic and biotic stresses.
source: The interaction affects plant growth (Rooney et al., 2009; Adolfsson et al., 2015) and resistance to various abiotic and biotic stresses (Pineda et al., 2010; Vannette et al., 2013; Chitarra et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Pineda et al., 2010; Vannette et al., 2013; Chitarra et al., 2016; Sharma et al., 2017.

claim: AMF interactions are physically restricted to the roots.
source: Although AMF interactions are physically restricted to the roots, they influence whole-plant performance, hence systemic metabolic responses have been anticipated, and searched for, but no general AMF-specific responses have been found (Bi et al., 2007; Toussaint, 2007; Schweiger and Müller, 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by citations.

claim: No general AMF-specific systemic metabolic responses have been found.
source: Although AMF interactions are physically restricted to the roots, they influence whole-plant performance, hence systemic metabolic responses have been anticipated, and searched for, but no general AMF-specific responses have been found (Bi et al., 2007; Toussaint, 2007; Schweiger and Müller, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Bi et al., 2007; Toussaint, 2007; Schweiger and Müller, 2015.

claim: Changes in foliar levels of carbohydrates, proteins, and amino acids, as well as secondary metabolites and phytohormones have been shown to respond to AMF inoculation.
source: While changes in foliar levels of carbohydrates, proteins, and amino acids, as well as secondary metabolites and phytohormones have been shown to respond to AMF inoculation (Schweiger et al., 2014; Aliferis et al., 2015; Adolfsson et al., 2017), these changes are not specific to AMF interactions and tend to be general responses to various abiotic and biotic stresses.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Schweiger et al., 2014; Aliferis et al., 2015; Adolfsson et al., 2017.

claim: Foliar metabolic changes in response to AMF inoculation are not specific to AMF interactions and tend to be general responses to various abiotic and biotic stresses.
source: While changes in foliar levels of carbohydrates, proteins, and amino acids, as well as secondary metabolites and phytohormones have been shown to respond to AMF inoculation (Schweiger et al., 2014; Aliferis et al., 2015; Adolfsson et al., 2017), these changes are not specific to AMF interactions and tend to be general responses to various abiotic and biotic stresses.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Large amounts of blumenol-type metabolites accumulate in roots after AMF inoculation.
source: In contrast, large amounts of blumenol-type metabolites accumulate in roots after AMF inoculation.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by subsequent citations and data in the manuscript.

claim: Blumenols are apocarotenoids, in particular C13 cyclohexenone derivatives, produced by the cleavage of carotenoids.
source: These compounds are apocarotenoids, in particular C13 cyclohexenone derivatives, produced by the cleavage of carotenoids.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by established knowledge of apocarotenoid biosynthesis.

claim: After AMF colonization, a C40 carotenoid is cleaved by carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase 7 (CCD7) to produce a C13 cyclohexenone and a C27 apocarotenoid.
source: After AMF colonization, a C40 carotenoid is cleaved by carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase 7 (CCD7) to produce a C13 cyclohexenone and a C27 apocarotenoid which is further cleaved by CCD1 to yield a second C13 cyclohexenone (Floss et al., 2008; Vogel et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Floss et al., 2008; Vogel et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2016.

claim: The C27 apocarotenoid is further cleaved by CCD1 to yield a second C13 cyclohexenone.
source: After AMF colonization, a C40 carotenoid is cleaved by carotenoid cleavage dioxygenase 7 (CCD7) to produce a C13 cyclohexenone and a C27 apocarotenoid which is further cleaved by CCD1 to yield a second C13 cyclohexenone (Floss et al., 2008; Vogel et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Floss et al., 2008; Vogel et al., 2010; Hou et al., 2016.

claim: Blumenols have been found to accumulate in the roots of AMF-colonized plants in a manner highly correlated with the fungal colonization rate.
source: The compounds have been found to accumulate in the roots of AMF-colonized plants in a manner highly correlated with the fungal colonization rate (Fester et al., 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Fester et al., 1999.

claim: Other stimuli such as pathogen infection and abiotic stresses do not induce blumenol accumulations in roots.
source: Other stimuli such as pathogen infection and abiotic stresses, do not induce their accumulations (Maier et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Maier et al., 1997.

claim: The AMF-induced accumulation of blumenols is widespread and has been observed in roots of plant species from different families, including mono- and dicotyledons.
source: The AMF-induced accumulation of these compounds is widespread and has been observed in roots of plant species from different families, including mono- and dicotyledons, (Hordeum vulgare, Peipp et al., 1997); Solanum lycopersicum and Nicotiana tabacum, Maier et al., 2000; e.g., Zea mays, Fester et al., 2002; Lotus japonicus and Medicago truncatula, Fester et al., 2005; Ornithogalum umbellatum, Schliemann et al., 2006; Allium porrum, Schliemann et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in various plant species.

claim: Only blumenol glycosides containing a blumenol C-based aglycone are positively correlated with mycorrhizal colonization.
source: However, previous studies have reported that only blumenol glycosides containing a blumenol C-based aglycone are positively correlated with mycorrhizal colonization.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by citations in the surrounding context.

claim: The blumenol C aglycone can be additionally hydroxylated at the C11 or carboxylated at the C11 or C12 position.
source: The aglycone can be additionally hydroxylated at the C11 or carboxylated at the C11 or C12 position (Maier et al., 1997; Maier et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maier et al., 1997 and Maier et al., 2000.

claim: 7,8-didehydro versions of blumenol C have been reported.
source: Additionally, 7,8-didehydro versions of blumenol C have been reported (Peipp et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Peipp et al., 1997.

claim: Blumenol glycosylation usually occurs as an O-glycoside at the C9 position.
source: The glycosylation usually occurs as an O-glycoside at the C9 position (Strack and Fester, 2006), but glycosylations at the hydroxylated C11 position have also been observed (Schliemann et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Strack and Fester, 2006.

claim: Blumenol glycosylations at the hydroxylated C11 position have been observed.
source: The glycosylation usually occurs as an O-glycoside at the C9 position (Strack and Fester, 2006), but glycosylations at the hydroxylated C11 position have also been observed (Schliemann et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schliemann et al., 2008.

claim: The glycosyl moiety of blumenols can be a single sugar or combinations of glucose (Glc), rhamnose, apiose, arabinose and/or glucuronic acid.
source: The glycosyl moiety can be a single sugar or combinations of glucose (Glc), rhamnose, apiose, arabinose and/or glucuronic acid, which, in turn can be additionally malonylated or contain a 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutarate decoration (Strack and Fester, 2006; Schliemann et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Strack and Fester, 2006 and Schliemann et al., 2008.

claim: The glycosyl moiety of blumenols can be additionally malonylated or contain a 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutarate decoration.
source: The glycosyl moiety can be a single sugar or combinations of glucose (Glc), rhamnose, apiose, arabinose and/or glucuronic acid, which, in turn can be additionally malonylated or contain a 3-hydroxy-3-methylglutarate decoration (Strack and Fester, 2006; Schliemann et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Strack and Fester, 2006 and Schliemann et al., 2008.

claim: The connections among sugar components in blumenols can vary (e.g., glucose-(1''→4')-glucose or glucose-(1''→6')-glucose).
source: The connections among sugar components can also vary (e.g., glucose-(1''→4')-glucose or glucose-(1''→6')-glucose; Maier et al., 2000; Fester et al., 2002).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Maier et al., 2000 and Fester et al., 2002.

claim: The particular type of blumenol decorations appears to be highly species-specific.
source: The particular type of decorations appears to be highly species-specific and it is likely that additional structural variants remain to be discovered.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by inference from the described structural diversity.

claim: Blumenols such as blumenol A, blumenol A-9-O-Glc, blumenol B, blumenol C and blumenol C-9-O-Glc were reported to occur in the aerial parts of various plant species.
source: Interestingly, blumenols such as blumenol A, blumenol A-9-O-Glc, blumenol B, blumenol C and blumenol C-9-O-Glc, were also reported to occur in the aerial parts of various plant species (Galbraith and Horn, 1972; Bhakuni et al., 1974; Takeda et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Galbraith and Horn, 1972; Bhakuni et al., 1974; Takeda et al., 1997.

claim: Most studies on blumenols in aerial parts focused on the identification of natural products using large scale extractions and were not performed in the context of AMF colonization.
source: However, most of these studies focused on the identification of natural products using large scale extractions (up to several kg of plant material) and were not performed in the context of AMF colonization.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by inference from the cited literature.

claim: Some blumenol compounds were found in plant families that are known to have lost their ability to establish AMF interactions (Brassicaceae and Urticaceae).
source: Furthermore, some blumenol compounds were also found in plant families that are known to have lost their ability to establish AMF interactions (Brassicaceae: Cutillo et al., 2005; Urticaceae: Aishan et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cutillo et al., 2005 and Aishan et al., 2010.

claim: These reports indicate AMF-independent constitutive levels of particular blumenols in aerial plant parts.
source: These reports indicate AMF-independent constitutive levels of particular blumenols in aerial plant parts.
evidence: The claim is an inference drawn from the cited literature showing blumenols in non-AMF plants.

claim: Adolfsson et al., 2017 analyzed blumenol accumulations together with other metabolites in leaves of plants with and without AMF colonization.
source: Adolfsson et al., 2017 analyzed blumenol accumulations together with other metabolites in leaves of plants with and without AMF colonization.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Adolfsson et al., 2017.

claim: None of the studies on foliar blumenols reported AMF-specific accumulations of blumenols or transcripts specific for their biosynthesis.
source: None of these studies reported AMF-specific accumulations of blumenols or transcripts specific for their biosynthesis.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by inference from the cited literature.

claim: The concentrations of some blumenol derivatives were reported to be down-regulated in response to AMF colonization.
source: The concentrations of some blumenol derivatives were even reported to be down-regulated in response to AMF colonization (Adolfsson et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Adolfsson et al., 2017.

claim: The characterization of AMF-associations is laborious and time-consuming, typically requiring destructive root harvesting and microscopic examination or transcript analyses.
source: The identification of a reliable metabolite marker in aerial plant tissues would be highly useful for AMF research since the characterization of AMF-associations is still laborious and time-consuming, typically requiring destructive root harvesting and microscopic examination or transcript analyses (Vierheilig et al., 2005; Parádi et al., 2010).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vierheilig et al., 2005 and Parádi et al., 2010.

claim: Five metabolites were annotated as blumenols: 11-hydroxyblumenol C-9-O-Glc (Compound 1), 11-carboxyblumenol C-9-O-Glc (Compound 2), 11-hydroxyblumenol C-9-O-Glc-Glc (Compound 3), blumenol C-9-O-Glc-Glc (Compound 4) and blumenol C-9-O-Glc (Compound 5).
source: Five metabolites were annotated as blumenols: 11-hydroxyblumenol C-9-O-Glc (Figure 2C; Compound 1), 11-carboxyblumenol C-9-O-Glc (Figure 2C; Compound 2), 11-hydroxyblumenol C-9-O-Glc-Glc (Compound 3), blumenol C-9-O-Glc-Glc (Compound 4) and blumenol C-9-O-Glc (Compound 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data from tandem-MS and NMR analysis as stated in the text.

claim: The abundance of the five blumenol C-glycosides continually increased with mycorrhizal development.
source: The abundance of the five blumenol C-glycosides continually increased with mycorrhizal development (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The abundance of the five blumenol C-glycosides was highly correlated with the mycorrhizal colonization rate as determined by the transcript abundances of classical arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis-marker genes.
source: and was highly correlated with the mycorrhizal colonization rate as determined by the transcript abundances of classical arbuscular mycorrhizal symbiosis-marker genes (fungal house-keeping gene, Ri-tub; plant marker genes, Vapyrin, RAM1, STR1 and PT4; Park et al., 2015; Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Data Set 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B and Data Set 1, and by citation to Park et al., 2015.

claim: Compounds 1 and 2 showed a similar AMF-specific accumulation in the leaves, as observed in the roots.
source: Compounds 1 and 2 showed a similar AMF-specific accumulation in the leaves, as observed in the roots (Figure 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Compounds 3 and 4 were not detected in leaves.
source: The other analyzed blumenols were not detected in leaves (Compounds 3 and 4; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Compound 5 showed a less consistent AMF-specific accumulation due to its constitutive background level.
source: or showed a less consistent AMF-specific accumulation (Compound 5; due to its constitutive background level; Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: At three weeks post inoculation, the abundance of compounds 1 and 2 in the leaves was sufficient to reflect the colonization level of the roots.
source: At three wpi, the abundance of compounds 1 and 2 in the leaves was sufficient to reflect the colonization level of the roots.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the kinetic experiment described in the text and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Classical AMF-marker-genes, which are usually analyzed in the roots, did not respond in the leaves.
source: In contrast, the classical AMF-marker-genes, which are usually analyzed in the roots, did not respond in the leaves (Figure 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4.

claim: In an inoculum-gradient experiment using increasing inoculum concentrations, proportionally higher Compound 1 and 2 levels were observed.
source: In an inoculum-gradient experiment using increasing inoculum concentrations, proportionally higher Compound 1 and 2 levels were observed (Figure 3B), accurately reflecting the differential colonization of roots across treatments (Figure 3E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3E.

claim: EV plants inoculated with natural inoculum (mainly consisting of Funneliformis mosseae and R. irregularis) accumulated Compounds 1 and 2 in leaves, while irCCaMK plants did not.
source: In addition to inoculation with a single AMF species (R. irregularis), we also tested mycorrhizal inoculum originally collected from the plant's native habitat, the Great Basin Desert in Utah, USA, which mainly consists of Funneliformis mosseae and R. irregularis. EV plants inoculated with this 'natural inoculum' also accumulated Compounds 1 and 2 in leaves, while irCCaMK plants did not (Figure 3C).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: When planted into the plant's natural environment in Utah, both EV and irCCaMK plants could be clearly distinguished by their leaf Compound 1 and 2 contents.
source: When planted into the plant's natural environment in Utah, both EV and irCCaMK plants could be clearly distinguished by their leaf Compound 1 and 2 contents. The signature of Compound 2 provided a better quality marker in these field-grown plants (Figure 3D, Figure 3—figure supplement 4).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 4.

claim: The foliar contents of Compounds 1 and 2 were highly correlated with the percentage of arbuscules in roots.
source: The foliar contents of these two compounds were highly correlated with the percentage of arbuscules in roots, the core structure of AMF interactions (Figure 3F, Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F and Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Biotic or abiotic stresses, including herbivory, pathogen infection and drought stress, did not elicit the foliar accumulations of Compounds 1 and 2.
source: In contrast, other biotic or abiotic stresses, including herbivory, pathogen infection and drought stress, did not elicit the foliar accumulations of Compounds 1 and 2 (Figure 5).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 5.

claim: AMF-specific blumenol signatures accumulated throughout the shoot, including different leaf positions, stem pieces, flowers and capsules.
source: An analysis of various plant tissues, including different leaf positions, stem pieces, flowers and capsules revealed that these AMF-specific signatures accumulated throughout the shoot (Figure 3G).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3G.

claim: Most of the candidate genes for blumenol biosynthesis were upregulated in roots, but not in leaves of N. attenuata plants in response to mycorrhizal colonization.
source: Blumenols are apocarotenoids originating from a side branch of the carotenoid pathway (Hou et al., 2016). Most of the candidate genes for blumenol biosynthesis were upregulated in roots, but not in leaves of N. attenuata plants in response to mycorrhizal colonization (Figure 6A, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, and by citation to Hou et al., 2016.

claim: AMF-indicative leaf apocarotenoids are transported from their site of synthesis in colonized roots to other plant parts.
source: We inferred that these AMF-indicative leaf apocarotenoids are transported from their site of synthesis in colonized roots to other plant parts.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observation that biosynthetic genes are upregulated in roots but not leaves, and is supported by subsequent experimental data.

claim: Blumenols occur in stem sap.
source: This is consistent with the occurrence of blumenols in stem sap (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) which was collected by centrifuging small stem pieces.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B.

claim: In DEX-treated leaves of i-irPDS plants showing PDS silencing, levels of the AMF-indicative Compounds 1 and 2 were not affected.
source: Treated leaves showed clear signs of bleaching, indicating PDS silencing (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), but levels of the AMF-indicative Compounds 1 and 2 were not affected, consistent with their transport from other tissues, likely the highly accumulating roots.
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: In DEX-treated leaves of i-irPDS plants, Compound 6 concentrations were reduced by nearly 40%, consistent with local production.
source: As a control, we analyzed the non-AMF-inducible Compound 6, showing constitutive levels in aerial tissues (Figure 6—figure supplement 2). In DEX-treated leaves, Compound 6 concentrations were reduced by nearly 40%, consistent with local production (Figure 6B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: After overnight incubation of roots in aqueous solutions of Compounds 1 or 2, the blumenol derivatives were clearly detected not only in roots, but also in shoots.
source: To confirm the within-plant transport potential of blumenols, we dipped roots of seedlings into aqueous solutions of Compounds 1 or 2. After overnight incubation, the blumenol derivatives were clearly detected not only in roots, but also in shoots (Figure 6C, Figure 6—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 6C and Figure 6—figure supplement 1E.

claim: A QTL analysis of 728 plants grown across a 7200 m2 field plot revealed that the abundance of Compound 2 mapped to a single locus on linkage group 3.
source: A QTL analysis of 728 plants grown across a 7200 m2 field plot (Figure 7D) revealed that the abundance of Compound 2 mapped to a single locus on linkage group 3 (Figure 7E)
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7D and Figure 7E.

claim: The QTL on linkage group 3 harbored a homologue of NOPE1 (NIATv7_g02911) previously shown to be required for the initiation of AMF symbioses in maize and rice.
source: which harbored a homologue of NOPE1 (NIATv7_g02911) previously shown to be required for the initiation of AMF symbioses in maize and rice (Nadal et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Nadal et al., 2017.

claim: Transcripts of NaNOPE1 were more abundant in AZ roots after AMF inoculation, but did not differ significantly in leaves.
source: Transcripts of NaNOPE1 were more abundant in AZ roots after AMF inoculation, but did not differ significantly in leaves (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B.

claim: AMF-specific accumulation of blumenol C-derivatives in roots is a widespread phenomenon within higher plants.
source: The AMF-specific accumulation of blumenol C-derivatives in roots is a widespread phenomenon within higher plants (Strack and Fester, 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Strack and Fester, 2006.

claim: An overlap in the AMF-specific blumenol responses in roots and leaves was found in Solanum lycopersicum, Triticum aestivum and Hordeum vulgare plants with and without AMF inoculation.
source: We analyzed Solanum lycopersicum, Triticum aestivum and Hordeum vulgare plants with and without AMF inoculation and again we found an overlap in the AMF-specific blumenol responses in roots and leaves, consistent with the transport hypothesis.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the analysis of these plant species as described in the text and shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Additional AMF-indicative blumenols were identified in the leaves of Medicago truncatula, Solanum tuberosum and Brachypodium distachyon.
source: Further analyses led to the identification of additional AMF-indicative blumenols in the leaves of Medicago truncatula, Solanum tuberosum and Brachypodium distachyon.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from the analysis of these plant species as described in the text and shown in Figure 7F.

claim: Various types of blumenols showed an AMF-specific accumulation in the shoot, including blumenol B (Compound 7), which has not previously been reported in an AMF-dependent context.
source: We identified various types of blumenols that showed an AMF-specific accumulation in the shoot, including blumenol B (Compound 7), which has not previously been reported in an AMF-dependent context (Figure 7F; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The particular blumenol types were species-dependent, but the general pattern was widespread across monocots and dicots.
source: As reported for roots, the particular blumenol types were species-dependent, but the general pattern was widespread across monocots and dicots in experiments conducted at different research facilities.
evidence: The claim is supported by data from experiments with multiple plant species shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The observed effects of AMF-specific blumenol accumulation were not found to be restricted to specific AMF taxa (R. irregularis, F. mosseae and Glomus versiforme).
source: In tests with diverse fungal species (R. irregularis, F. mosseae and Glomus versiforme), the observed effects were not found to be restricted to specific AMF taxa (Figure 7F; Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: AMF interactions are proposed to have played an important role for the colonization of land by plants.
source: AMF-interactions are proposed to have played an important role for the colonization of land by plants and still play an important role for a majority of plants by improving the function of their roots and increasing whole-plant performance.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: AMF interactions still play an important role for a majority of plants by improving the function of their roots and increasing whole-plant performance.
source: AMF-interactions are proposed to have played an important role for the colonization of land by plants and still play an important role for a majority of plants by improving the function of their roots and increasing whole-plant performance.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Characteristic transcriptional and metabolic changes have been observed in the roots of AMF-colonized plants.
source: Consequently, the investigation of AMF-mediated effects on a host plant's physiology has been an important research field for many decades and characteristic transcriptional and metabolic changes have been observed in the roots of AMF-colonized plants.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: The cumbersome analysis of AMF-interactions restrains large-scale investigations and commercial applications.
source: However, the cumbersome analysis of AMF-interactions, involving destructive harvesting of root tissues and microscopic or transcript analysis, restrains large-scale investigations and commercial applications.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by inference from the described limitations of current methods.

claim: AMF interactions affect the primary and secondary metabolism in the systemic, aerial tissues of plants.
source: AMF interactions were also shown to affect the primary and secondary metabolism in the systemic, aerial tissues of plants; however none of these responses proved to be widespread and sufficiently specific to function as reliable markers (Schweiger and Müller, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schweiger and Müller, 2015.

claim: None of the systemic metabolic responses to AMF proved to be widespread and sufficiently specific to function as reliable markers.
source: AMF interactions were also shown to affect the primary and secondary metabolism in the systemic, aerial tissues of plants; however none of these responses proved to be widespread and sufficiently specific to function as reliable markers (Schweiger and Müller, 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schweiger and Müller, 2015.

claim: Metabolites and metabolite responses are often specific to particular parts and tissues of a plant.
source: Metabolites and metabolite responses are often specific to particular parts and tissues of a plant (Li et al., 2016; Lee et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Li et al., 2016 and Lee et al., 2017.

claim: Local metabolic responses can spread to other plant parts.
source: but it is also known that local responses can spread to other plant parts.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by established scientific knowledge.

claim: Metabolites do not only accumulate at their place of biosynthesis but can be readily transported throughout the plant.
source: Additionally, metabolites do not only accumulate at their place of biosynthesis but can be readily transported throughout the plant (Baldwin, 1989).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Baldwin, 1989.

claim: The confirmation of compound identities in leaf samples with high resolution MS techniques proved to be challenging and required additional sample purification steps.
source: Interestingly, the confirmation of compound identities in leaf samples with high resolution MS techniques proved to be challenging and required additional sample purification steps.
evidence: The claim is stated directly in the text and is supported by the described experimental procedures.

claim: Matrix effects likely thwarted the detection of AMF-indicative, systemic blumenol responses in previous investigations.
source: Likely, such matrix effects thwarted the detection of these AMF-indicative, systemic blumenol responses in previous investigations.
evidence: The claim is an inference based on the observed challenges in detecting these compounds in leaf samples.

claim: Under the experimental conditions, AMF-indicative blumenols began mirroring the colonization rates of roots at around three weeks post inoculation.
source: Under our conditions, AMF-indicative blumenols began mirroring the colonization rates of roots at around three wpi (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Microscopic methods can detect first signs of AMF colonization of the roots already after a few days.
source: Although microscopic methods can detect first signs of AMF colonization of the roots already after a few days (Brundrett et al., 1985)
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Brundrett et al., 1985.

claim: The sensitivity of the blumenol-based method was found to be sufficient to analyze colonization rates observed in the glasshouse and in nature.
source: the sensitivity of our method was found to be sufficient to analyze colonization rates observed in the glasshouse and, more importantly, in nature (Figures 3 and 7).
evidence: The claim is supported by data shown in Figures 3 and 7.

claim: The analysis of AMF-indicative blumenols in the shoot provides a convenient, easy-to-use, and minimally destructive tool to interrogate plant-AMF interactions in a HTP manner.
source: We propose that the analysis of AMF-indicative blumenols in the shoot provides a convenient, easy-to-use, and minimally destructive tool to interrogate plant-AMF interactions in a HTP manner that allows for forward genetic studies even under field conditions (Figure 7E) and empowers plant breeding programs to produce mycorrhiza-responsive and P-efficient high-yielding lines (van de Wiel et al., 2016).
